newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Nazi hunter Wiesenthal determined to carry on.
newsitem.headline: Nazi hunter Wiesenthal determined to carry on.

text.p: Veteran Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal, at 88 showing no signs of slowing down, said on Monday his work tracking down war criminals must go on.
Wiesenthal, speaking at the German launch of a biography entitled "A Life in Search of Justice" by British author Hella Pick, said the atrocities of the past must never be forgotten.
"My work is a warning to the murderers of tomorrow. They should know that we persecute today the crimes of more than 50 years ago," he told reporters.
Wiesenthal, a survivor of the Holocaust, claims to have helped to bring more than 1,000 escaped Nazis to book in the past 50 years.

Pick said he had a relentless sense of duty to truth and justice. "The importance of Wiesenthal is that he confronts us with the deepest moral issues of the time and the meaning of justice and forgiveness," she said.
"He has achieved enormous strides in bringing understanding of the Holocaust to new generations as well as to older ones."
Wiesenthal emerged from the Austrian concentration camp of Mauthausen, west of Vienna, severely emaciated and with few surviving relatives.
"I wanted to live for just 15 minutes more after I was liberated to see that the Nazis really had lost the war," he said.
When he was well enough he went to Nuremberg and began pouring over 110,000 tonnes of German documents in the hope of uncovering evidence to track down Nazi suspects.
In 1947 he set up the Jewish Documentation Centre in Linz, which then moved to Vienna in 1961.
Wiesenthal recounted how, after he was the victim of a failed bomb attack and numerous death threats, his wife begged him to leave and start a new life in Israel.
"'Our office is the last in the world,' I said. 'Can I close my office? I will seem like a traitor and as far as I know you you would not want to live with a traitor.'"

Wiesenthal said he was gratified when then Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky said in 1994 Austria must accept that it was not merely an innocent victim but also a perpetrator of horrors committed by the Nazis.
For most of the post-war era Austria sought to present itself as the first victim of Hitler's aggression.
Vienna's Jewish community numbered around 200,000 before World War Two. By 1945 only around 200 Jews remained.
